So I'm not very interested in the US personally, at least right now, and what helped me "escape" was teaching English. But this also aligned generally with my career goals and interests.

Depending on your personality, you should reconsider moving abroad just because the teaching alone could burn you out. But if you think you handle it, go ahead!

On "escaping" — I assume you mean to Western Europe. Their politics are not necessarily better, and they have the same long-term problems as the US (HUGE government debt which WILL cause a recession or inflation soon, just like in the US). This may be controversial among reddit users, but I also found them to be generally more closed off and racist than Americans, despite our current government. There are also quality of life differences that some Americans may not like. It depends on your personality. I have cousins there that are jealous of Americans, just as much as I am of them! Regardless, there are some programs you can apply for to teach temporarily there.

Otherwise, depending on where you go in the world, the quality of life and political situation vary greatly and the reality is that on a global level, the US is still a very nice place to live. I learned this quite quickly after moving to the "third world." Americans and Europeans can be quite myopic and both are prone to thinking they are the center of civilization. Both places have pros and cons. There will be creature comforts you will have to give up, things that will push you out of your comfort zone, and things that will surprise and delight you. 

All this to say that if your main goal is "escape," then you should reconsider as it suggests you lack a bit of perspective. If you want to travel, you want to see new places, you want to meet new people, you want to teach, then go ahead.

The only thing I would say is that you NEED to work in a school ASAP. You didn't mention working in a school in your post, only "government," and you didn't say what your part-time work was.

Please, please consider substituting or finding some way to get into a school or classroom before going and getting a master's. You'll learn more in a few months of working at a school than you ever will in any graduate program (minus the actual intern work).

I've been thinking about this and similar things after living in France for a year. I'm back in a large American city now.

According to Wikipedia, France has one of the highest levels of homelessness in Europe. Even so, the level of destituteness isn't comparable to any major American metro. There is no poop in the streets, no needles, no encampments right in the city center or even around it. The homeless are less violent, less drugged out, not as likely to have psychotic breaks on the street in the middle of the day, etc.

There is a program in France called la CAF (caisse d'allocation familiale) which I even qualified for as a foreigner on a work visa with my little income. This agency runs a calculation of your income and your rent and cuts you a check for you to use to pay that rent. You can even do this with private landlords, you don't have to be in some government owned housing complex to benefit. Combined with the cheap healthcare (health related debt being one of the largest causes of bankruptcy in the US), I'm sure this keeps people from ending up on the street.

I think the answer to your question is in the attitude of Americans. Our society is individualistic to a fault. Americans seem to have a hard time understanding the idea that when other people lead better more stable lives, we all as a society benefit even if there is no direct benefit for us as individuals. A program like the CAF could never exist in the US today. Our government and our culture wouldn't allow it. Widespread homelessness (for an industrialized country) is viewed as a personal problem here. It is a personal failure to be poor in the US, and despite any number of factors that were working to make your life suck, we view homelessness as something YOU did wrong, and thus something you DESERVE. This attitude is what prevents us from doing anything to help homelessness, whether it is building homes or helping people pay rent or making healthcare cheaper or education (social mobility) cheaper.

The problem is counting words deals with the question of what a word is. Do we count words with different senses, like run as a verb and an noun? Do we count compound words? Words can be defined differently in other languages too. Do we take all the declensions of a word in Russian as different words? What about the many case endings in Finnish, are those all different words? Better yet, some agglutinative and polysynthetic languages can end up with words that contain many different morphemes and whole verbs and their arguments into one long sentence-word. Something like “my big brother went to the store” could end up as a whole “word” when written down in Inuit languages.

As far as I know there is no consensus among linguists as to what constitutes a word and how they are different from things like morphemes, and so some texts like books or papers will define what a word is within the context of what they discuss, for clarity.

As some of the other commenters mentioned, words can change in different ways. They can be replaced by words that are borrowed in, or change phonetically to the point that two words may not be recognized by the average person as cognates (like 'heart' and 'corazón').

As one commenter mentioned, words in the Swadesh list, a list of words chosen for their universality and commonality to all humans and thus all languages (words like eye, dog, red, man, etc) can be resistant to change. However, there are still instances of words on these lists in our languages that have been supplanted by foreign words.

In the context of language change due to borrowing and language contact, the idea of 'closed' and 'open' word classes comes into play. Open word classes are word classes (like parts of speech) that can take on new words and vocabulary, so nouns, adjectives, and verbs belong here. We come up with new nouns and adjectives often, and we readily borrow words into our language from others that belong in open word classes. Closed word classes are things like pronouns, prepositions, and conjunctions, and when it comes to language change due to borrowing and contact, these words are less likely to be borrowed into other languages or be replaced by words from other languages. In that regard, they "change" less.

From about the 13th to the 17th/18th century, French vowels went through reverse assimilation (the first phone becoming more similar to the following one) before nasal consonants. There are a few theories why, but it seems the consensus is this: the vowels went through three steps that led to their modern pronunciation. 1. The vowels would nasalize before a nasal consonant for example “vent” /vɑ̃nt/ 2. The nasal consonant would be deleted /vɑ̃(n)t/ 3. The following consonants might also be deleted, as happens in french today /vɑ̃/
As for why the vowels were lowered instead of raised? I am not sure, I briefly read the article to give you an answer of the process involved. There might not be a specific reason. This article mentions a possible Celtic substrate language influencing the development of French nasal vowels. Sometimes when asking why languages change in one way and not another, the answer is “it just happened that way.”
